title: Is There a Government Final Expense Program? | Honorbrook
description: No. There is no federal final expense insurance program for the general public. Ads describe private life insurance. See which public benefits do exist.
h1_html: Is there a government final expense program?
lead: No. There is no federal final expense insurance program for the general public. The “programs” advertised to the public on TV and in the mail are private life insurance, sold by insurance companies and licensed agents.
article_html:
The federal government does not sell or give final expense insurance to the general public. When a TV ad, a postcard or a caller offers the public a “final expense program,” it is describing private life insurance that you apply for and pay for.

Final expense insurance is a real product. The policies in these ads are not a government benefit. Here is what the ad wording means, which public benefits exist, and what to ask before you share your information.

What “state-regulated” means

Federal law leaves the regulation of insurance mainly to the states. The law says the business of insurance “shall be subject to the laws of the several States” (15 U.S.C. 1012). Your state insurance department oversees the insurance companies and agents that do business in your state.

So every life insurance policy lawfully sold in your state is “state-regulated.” The phrase does not mean the state runs the plan, pays for it or picked you for it. The Minnesota Attorney General’s office explains: “all insurance companies are regulated by the state, so a ‘state-regulated’ plan is nothing new or special.”

The District of Columbia’s insurance department made a similar point about one mailed “benefit information” form. It told residents: “this is not an opportunity to receive District government-sponsored funeral insurance.”

A mention of Social Security in an ad does not mean Social Security sent or approved it. Section 1140 of the Social Security Act bars companies from “giving a false impression of association with, or authorization or endorsement by, the Social Security Administration.”

In short: “State-regulated” describes the rules a seller must follow, not who pays. With private final expense insurance, you pay the premium. The insurance company, not the government, pays claims under the policy’s terms.

Public benefits that do exist

A few public benefits can help after a death.

BenefitWho it is forWhat the agency says
Social Security lump-sum death paymentA spouse. A spouse who lived in another home may be eligible in some cases. If there is no spouse, some children: age 17 or younger, ages 18–19 and in school (K–12) full time, or any age if they developed a disability at age 21 or younger.“A spouse might get a one-time death benefit payment of $255.” You must apply within 2 years of the death. (ssa.gov, as stated on November 25, 2026.)
VA burial allowancesA person who pays for an eligible veteran’s burial and funeral, if VA’s requirements are met.Allowances “help cover some of the costs of the burial, funeral, and plot or interment.” VA lists who qualifies and the current amounts. (va.gov, updated October 30, 2026.)
VA life insuranceVeterans, service members and their families.One plan, VALife, is whole life insurance for veterans with service-connected disabilities. (va.gov, updated November 24, 2026; VALife page, October 13, 2026.)
State or local burial helpDepends on where you live. Programs differ and can end.Michigan says “burial payment assistance may be available” when the estate and other funds “are not sufficient.” The District of Columbia’s human services department says that as of September 30, 2025 it “will no longer provide Burial Assistance funds.”

None of these is a final expense insurance policy for the general public. Honorbrook is a private insurance agency. It is not connected with Social Security, VA or any other government agency.

For who pays when there is no policy, see how much a funeral costs and who pays. Veterans can also read life insurance for veterans.

How to check an agent’s license

State insurance regulators work together through the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC). Its consumer advice is plain: “Make sure the agent and insurance company are licensed in your state.”

  1. Ask for the agent’s full name, the agency name and the National Producer Number (NPN). An NPN is an ID number assigned during licensing.
  2. Open the NAIC’s Insurance Departments page. Under “Find an Insurance Agent,” choose your state to reach its agent search.
  3. Confirm the agent holds a license in your state.

You can check us the same way. Our agent, Luay Sadqi, holds NPN 21370662. Our state pages, such as Virginia and Maryland, name each regulator.

Questions to ask any caller or mailer

These are fair questions for anyone who contacts you, including us.

  1. Who are you, and are you licensed in my state? Ask for the name and NPN, then check them.
  2. Which insurance company would issue the policy? Ask whether that company is licensed in your state too.
  3. Is this insurance that I pay for? Ask plainly whether the offer is connected to any government agency.
  4. What happens to my information? Ask who will get your name, age and phone number, and who will contact you.
  5. When does the full benefit start? Ask whether the policy pays the full amount from the first day or has a waiting period. See graded death benefits explained.
  6. Can I have it in writing first? Ask for the company name, the premium and the policy terms in writing before you give bank details.

For questions about price and policy terms, read the hidden costs of final expense insurance.

If you want coverage

Whether you qualify, what you pay and what a policy pays depend on your age, health, state and the insurance company. A policy’s promises depend on the claims-paying ability of the company that issues it. Our page on final expense life insurance explains how it works. You can also ask for a final expense quote.

This article is general education, not legal, tax or insurance advice.

Sources

Each page was read on November 25, 2026. A date is listed where the page shows one.

  • U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs: Veterans burial allowance, updated October 30, 2026; VA life insurance, updated November 24, 2026; VALife, updated October 13, 2026.
  • United States Code, 15 U.S.C. 1012. 2024 edition.
  • Minnesota Attorney General, Protect Your Personal Information from Marketers.

  • SSA Office of the Inspector General, Consumer Protection: Section 1140.
  • Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, Burial.
  • DC Department of Human Services, Burial Assistance. Notice effective September 30, 2025.
  • NAIC, How to Choose an Insurance Agent, February 1, 2019; Insurance Departments and Life Insurance.
  • National Insurance Producer Registry, Look up a National Producer Number.
  • Medicare.gov, Parts of Medicare.

faq.q: Is there a government final expense program for seniors?
faq.a: No. There is no federal final expense insurance program for the general public. Ads that use the word program describe private life insurance that you apply for and pay for. Social Security has a one-time death payment for some survivors, and VA has burial allowances and life insurance for eligible veterans.

faq.q: What does state-regulated final expense insurance mean?
faq.a: It means the insurance company and the agent must follow state insurance law, as every insurer doing business in the state must. It does not mean the state runs the plan or pays for it. The Minnesota Attorney General's office says a state-regulated plan is nothing new or special.

faq.q: Does Social Security pay a death benefit for funeral costs?
faq.a: Social Security has a lump-sum death payment. Its website, ssa.gov, describes it as a one-time payment intended to help cover costs when a spouse or parent dies. As ssa.gov states it on November 25, 2026, a spouse might get a one-time death benefit payment of $255. If there is no spouse, some children may be eligible. You must apply within 2 years of the death.

faq.q: Is the final expense program I saw on TV real?
faq.a: The ads are for private life insurance, which is a real product. It is not a government benefit. Before you share personal information, ask who the agent is and which insurance company would issue the policy. Then check the agent's license with your state insurance department.

faq.q: How do I check if an insurance agent is licensed?
faq.a: Ask for the agent's full name and National Producer Number. Then use your state insurance department's agent search. The NAIC Insurance Departments page links to each state's search. The NAIC's advice is to make sure the agent and the insurance company are licensed in your state.

faq.q: Is final expense insurance part of Medicare?
faq.a: No. Final expense insurance is private life insurance. Medicare.gov describes Medicare as federal health insurance for people age 65 and older and for some younger people with certain disabilities or conditions. Medicare Part A is hospital insurance, Part B is medical insurance and Part D is drug coverage. For questions about what Medicare covers, go to medicare.gov.

facts.claim: HEADLINE ANSWER (a negative, so no single source states it in one sentence): there is no federal final expense insurance program for the general public; the 'programs' offered to the public in ads and mailers are private life insurance. Basis: the Minnesota Attorney General and the DC insurance regulator say these mailings do not come from government and are used to sell private insurance (this entry and the next three); Social Security's own death payment is a one-time $255 (ssa.gov entries below); VA life insurance is for Veterans, service members and their families (va.gov entries below). The checker searched regulator and federal sites on November 25, 2026 and found no federal final expense insurance program for the general public. No source read covers TV ads by name; that part follows from the same reasoning.
